thread.title: Double Features 010: Kathryn Bigelow, part 2

author: Katherine Nabity
title: Double Features 010: Kathryn Bigelow, part 2
text:
Welcome to Double Features!
For these posts, I’ll watch two movies—maybe they are obviously related, maybe they’re not—and then I’ll decide whether they would make a good double feature.
Until I looked at my spreadsheet, I hadn’t realized that my first Double Features post was also Kathryn Bigelow. So, here we go: part 2!
K-19: The Widowmaker
Year: 2002
Runtime: 2h 18m
Rated: PG-13
Writers: Christopher Kyle, Louis Nowra
Director: Kathryn Bigelow
Stars: Harrison Ford, Liam Neeson, Peter Sarsgaard
In 1961, the Soviet Union raced to get its nuclear submarine sea-worthy and on the board. It didn’t go well, not that the world would know for 30 years. Based on a true story.
K-19: The Widowmaker is somewhat misbegotten. We can start with the title. I’d like to know what went on behind the scenes concerning this name. K-19 would probably have been perfectly fine title. The Widowmaker? Also solid, although, historically, that wasn’t the sub’s nickname.* Put them together with a colon and it makes this movie feel like it’s a cheap sequel or something. (*The sub’s nickname was Hiroshima, which of course would not have worked as a title.)
Next, we have the accents. Harrison Ford seemingly can do a Harrison Ford accent and that is all. Liam Neeson gives up after a few scenes. Honestly, that is less distracting. Perhaps worse is the very clunky dialogue. Beyond formal, the way characters speak is stiff and didactic. The early portion of the film is too procedural; we’re never given enough interactions between the “smaller” characters to be fully invested in their fates.
There is about an hour of a good movie here when things go very wrong. Potential catastrophes start to pile up and character rise to meet the challenges. Bigelow is good at choreographing action even when the actions are quite small.
A House of Dynamite
Year: 2025
Runtime: 1h 52m
Rated: R
Writer: Noah Oppenheim
Director: Kathryn Bigelow
Stars: Idris Elba, Rebecca Ferguson, Gabriel Basso, Jared Harris, Tracy Letts
An intercontinental ballistic missile is launched by an unknown assailant. In 20 minutes, it will hit Chicago. How will the US respond?
A House of Dynamite follows the same events through three different timelines, each separated by a title card. I was unaware of the format of going in, but is pretty easy to follow along with. The three timelines follow different levels of the response team from the Army officers who originally detect the missile in the first section to the President of the United States deciding on level of retaliation in the last section. For me, this mostly worked very well. Each section adds information about the situation that we didn’t have before. By the third time through, I began to feel the weight of repetition baring down on the story and was happy it went no further.
All in all, I really enjoyed A House of Dynamite. Kathryn Bigelow has a penchant for examining characters in the midst of situations, and this might be her quintessential example of that. It’s tense. We meet many characters over the not-even two hour runtime, but we’re given enough glimpses into who they are to care about them. The performances are across the board good, and it’s a wide board. Also, no spoilers, but I don’t see how this movie could have ended any other way than it did.
Would these be a good Double Feature?
No. K-19 is way too slow of a movie to double up with anything else. This is an interesting duo of movies, considering both involve Russian/US politics and possible nuclear war over 60 years apart, but I wouldn’t watch them back-to-back.
K-19 includes some of the same hallmarks of A House of Dynamite: a group of people who are “prepared” for a situation they really don’t want to find themselves in. Unfortunately, K-19 doesn’t handle its characters as deftly. A better Kathryn Bigelow double feature might be The Hurt Locker and A House of Dynamite. The Hurt Locker (Bigelow’s next film after K-19) investigates “characters in a situation” from the other side of the coin. Sergeant James absolutely wants to be (maybe even needs to be) in the situations he’s in. Every single character in A House of Dynamite wants to be any where else.
